preamble: The voiceless dental affricate [ts] of medieval Ibero-Romance and northern Italo-Romance became the interdental fricative [θ] in several varieties. The change is indirect: the affricate first lost its stop phase, giving a dental sibilant [s̪], and this sibilant was then fronted to a non-sibilant interdental [θ]. Castilian Spanish is the classic case, and Galician and conservative Venetan dialects (Bellunese, north Trevisan) did the same independently.

examples.note: By 1600 /t͡s̪/ had deaffricated and merged with the /s̪/ from devoiced /d͡z̪/. This dental sibilant was later fronted to interdental /θ/, the basis of modern distinción.
In Middle Galician the affricates deaffricated, with different results in the west and the east. The central and eastern dialects have /θ/, while the western dialects have seseo: [ˈsiŋkʊ], [ˈlus].
The historical ç/z letters are realized as [s], [ts] or [θ] depending on dialect. Bellunese, north Trevisan and some rural central varieties have the interdental fricative.
Thao /θ/ is written ⟨th⟩ in the practical orthography and ⟨c⟩ in Blust's dictionary, so cumay is [θumaj].

sources: Penny, R. (2002). A History of the Spanish Language (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511992827
